State whether one level page table is sufficient for virtual to physical translation. Provide a valid reason for the same. Given: • Virtual Address: 32bit • Page size:1KB page size
questions.answer: No it is not possible to maintain a one level page table for virtual to physical translation Reason: the large memory overhead in maintaining page tables Explanation: Size of page table = (total number of page table entries) *(size of a page table entry) Let us see how many entries are there in page table Number of entries in page table = (virtual address space size)/(page size) = (2^32)/(2^10) = 2^22 Now, let us see how big each entry is. If size of physical memory is 512 MB then number of bits required to address a byte in 512 MB is 29. So, there will be (512MB)/(1KB) = (2^29)/(2^10) page frames in physical memory. To address a page frame 19 bits are required. Therefore, each entry in page table is required to have 19 bits. Note that page table entry also holds auxiliary information about the page such as a present bit, a dirty or modified bit, address space or process ID information, amongst others. So size of page table > (total number of page table entries) *(size of a page table entry) > (2^22 *19) bytes > 9.5 MB And this much memory is required for each process because each process maintains its own page table. Also, size of page table will be more for physical memory more than 512MB. Therefore, it is advised to use multilevel page table for such scenarios.

questions.answer: Addressing within a 1024-word page requires 10 bits because 1024 = 210. Since the logical address space consists of 64 = 26 pages, the logical addresses must be 10+6 = 16 bits. Similarly, since there are 32 = 25 physical frames, physical addresses are 5 + 10 = 15 bits long.

questions.text: Explain Belady’s Anomaly and also state the reasons behind Belady’s Anomaly?
questions.answer: Belady’s Anomaly is the phenomenon of increasing the number of page faults on increasing the number of frames in main memory. Reason Behind Belady’s Anomaly- An algorithm suffers from Belady’s Anomaly if and only if it does not follow stack property. Algorithms that follow stack property are called as stack based algorithms. Stack based algorithms do not suffer from Belady’s Anomaly. This is because these algorithms assign priority to a page for replacement that is independent of the number of frames in the main memory.

questions.text: Race conditions are possible in many computer systems. Consider a banking system that maintains an account balance with two functions: deposit(amount) and withdraw(amount). These two functions are passed the amount that is to be deposited or withdraw... Describe how a race condition is possible and what might be done to prevent the race condition from occurring
questions.answer: Assume that the balance in the account is $250.00 and that the husband calls withdraw($50) and the wife calls deposit($100). Obviously, the correct value should be $300.00. Since these two transactions will be serialized, the local value of the balance for the husband becomes $200.00, but before he can commit the transaction, the deposit(100) operation takes place and updates the shared value of the balance to $300.00. We then switch back to the husband, and the value of the shared balance is set to $200.00—obviously an incorrect value

questions.answer: Accessing data more quickly can be accomplished through paging. questions.text: Explain demand paging?
questions.answer: Demand paging is a method that loads pages into memory on demand. This method is mostly used in virtual memory. In this, a page is only brought into memory when a location on that particular page is referenced during execution.

questions.text: List the steps needed to handle page fault.
questions.answer: 1. The memory address requested is first checked, to make sure it was a valid memory request. 2. If the reference was invalid, the process is terminated. Otherwise, the page must be paged in. 3. A free frame is located, possibly from a free-frame list. 4. A disk operation is scheduled to bring in the necessary page from disk. 5. When the I/O operation is complete, the process’s page table is updated with the new frame number, and the invalid bit is changed to indicate that this is now a valid page reference. 6. The instruction that caused the page fault must now be restarted from the beginning, ( as soon as this process gets another turn on the CPU. )

questions.text: Q23. What conditions must be met in order to solve the critical-section problem?
questions.answer:
The requirements are: 1. Mutual exclusion. If process Pi is executing in its critical 
section, then no other processes can be executing in their critical section. 2. Progress. If no 
process is executing in its critical section and some processes wish to enter their critical section, 
then only those processes that are not executing in their remainder sections can participate in the 
decision on which will enter its CS next, and this selection cannot be postponed indefinitely. (No 
process should have to wait forever to enter its critical section. 3. Bounded waiting. There exists 
a bound, or limit, on the number of times that other processes are allowed to enter their critical 
sections after a process has made a request to enter its critical section and before that request is 
granted.

questions.text: Q29. In the following code, pthread_mutex_t lock = PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER; pthread_cond_t init = PTHREAD_COND_INITIALIZER; Pthread_mutex_lock(&lock); while (initialized == 0) Pthread_cond_wait(&init, &lock); Pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock); The code text to see whether the variable initialized has been set to 0, then calls the wait routine to sleep until the other thread wakes it up. The following is the awaking code, Pthread_mutex_lock(&lock); initialized = 1; Pthread_cond_signal(&init); Pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock); You might have noticed that the wait call takes a lock as its second input, but the signal call only takes a condition. Explain.
questions.answer: The reason is that the wait call, in addition to putting the calling thread to sleep, releases the lock when putting told the caller to sleep. Otherwise how could another thread acquire the lock and signal it to wake up? However, before returning after being woken, the pthread_cond_wait() re-acquires the lock, thus ensuring that anytime the waiting thread is running between the lock acquired at the beginning of the wait sequence and the lock release at the end, it holds the lock.

questions.text: Q30. Disabling interrupts was one of the earlier methods proposed for the implementation of locks. Discuss the flaws in this approach.
questions.answer: This approach allows any calling thread to perform a preview of a pre-village operation (turning interrupts on and off), which is quite a risky thing. A greedy program could call lock() at the beginning of its execution and thus monopolize the processor or a malicious program could call lock() and go into an endless loop, and OS will never regain its control of the system. This method will not work in multiprocessor scenarios. If multiple threads are running on different CPUs and each tries to enter the same critical section, even if the interrupts are disabled, the threads will be able to run on other processors and can enter the critical section. This approach can be inefficient. Compared to normal instruction execution, code that masks or unmasks interrupts tends to be executed slowly by modern CPUs.

questions.text: Q31. What are the main conditions that an efficient lock is expected to fulfill?
questions.answer: The first and foremost task of a lock is to provide mutual exclusion (i.e. preventing multiple threads from entering a critical section). To make sure that each thread contending for the lock get a fair shot at acquiring it once it is free. None of the threads starve. Finally check its performance. There are two cases here. First, is, when a single thread is running and grabs and releases the lock, what is the overhead of doing so? Another is the case where multiple threads are contending for the lock on a single CPU.

questions.text: Problem4: A shared variable x, initialized to zero, is operated on by four concurrent processes W, X, Y, Z as follows. Each of the processes W and X reads x from memory, increments by one, stores it to memory and then terminates. Each of the processes Y and Z reads x from memory, decrements by two, stores it to memory, and then terminates. Each process before reading x invokes the P operation (i.e. wait) on a counting semaphore S and invokes the V operation (i.e. signal) on the semaphore S after storing x to memory. Semaphore S is initialized to two. What is the maximum possible value of x after all processes complete execution?
questions.answer: The maximum possible value of x after all processes complete execution is 2

questions.text:
Step-04:
● Process W gets scheduled again.
● It resumes its execution from where it left.
● Before preemption it had already read the value x = 0.
● Now, it increments the value of x by 1. Now, x = 0 + 1 = 1.
● It writes the value x = 1 in the memory.
● It executes the signal(S) operation and the value of S increments by 1. Now, S = 2.
● Now, execution of process W is completed.

Step-05:
● Process X arrives.
● It executes the wait(S) operation and the value of S decrements by 1. Now, S = 1.
● It reads the value x = 1.
● It increments the value of x by 1. Now, x = 1 + 1 = 2.
● It writes the value x = 2 in the memory.
● It executes the signal(S) operation and the value of S increments by 1. Now, S = 2.
● Now, execution of process X is completed.

Thus,
● Final value of x = 2.
● This is the maximum possible value of x that can be achieved after executing all the 4 processes.
● Option (D) is correct.

questions.text: 10) How would you improve performance when using semaphores?
questions.answer:
1. Use a lock‑free algorithm – this will allow your program to avoid the overhead of acquiring and releasing locks.
2. Use a priority queue – this will ensure that the threads with the highest priority are able to acquire the semaphore first.
3. Use a fair semaphore – this will ensure that all threads have a fair chance of acquiring the semaphore, instead of one thread hogging the semaphore and preventing other threads from making progress.

questions.text: Q9. What is Deadlock?
questions.answer: Deadlock is a situation when two or more processes wait for each other to finish and none of them ever finish. Consider an example when two trains are coming toward each other on same track and there is only one track, none of the trains can move once they are in front of each other. Similar situation occurs in operating systems when there are two or more processes hold some resources and wait for resources held by other(s).

questions.text: Q10. A system is having 3 user processes P1, P2 and P3 where P1 requires 21 units of resource R, P2 requires 31 units of resource R, P3 requires 41 units of resource R. The minimum number of units of R that ensures no deadlock is ?
questions.answer: In worst case, the number of units that each process holds = one less than its maximum demand. So, • Process P1 holds 20 units of resource R • Process P2 holds 30 units of resource R • Process P3 holds 40 units of resource R. Thus, • Maximum number of units of resource R that ensures deadlock = 20 + 30 + 40 = 90. Minimum number of units of resource R that ensures no deadlock = 90 + 1 = 91.

questions.text: Q11. How to prevent deadlock?
questions.answer:
1. Mutual Exclusion: When you have sharable resources, there will be no fight for resources, which will prevent deadlock conditions.
2. Hold and Wait: In this condition, a process holding resources is waiting for other resources. Ways to eliminate this condition:
   a) When the process beforehand specifies the resources it requires. In this way, the process doesn’t have to wait for allocation.
   b) By releasing all the resources the process is currently holding and then making a new request.
3. No pre-emption: Preemption means temporary interruption of program execution. Normally processes can’t be preempted. Suppose some process P1 wants a resource R1 held by process P2. This situation will lead to a deadlock state. But to avoid deadlock, the process P2 is preempted, and resource R1 could be released and given to process P1. Then we can prevent deadlock.
4. Circular Wait: We can eliminate this circular wait condition by giving priority to each resource. A process accesses the resources in increasing order of priority. If a request is made for a low‑priority resource (being held by some other resource), the request will be considered invalid.

Q16. Vaibhav, Suraj and Uday go to a Chinese restaurant. But they go there at 8 pm (Busy time). So, waiter apologize and says he can provide only 2 pairs of chopsticks (i.e., four chopsticks), which need to be share between 3 friends.  Now, Vaibhav come up with an idea. He suggests to put all four chopsticks in an empty glass at center table & each diner should obey the following protocol: while ( ! had_enough_to_eat() ) { aquire_one_chopstick(); aquire_one_chopstick(); eat(); release_one_chopstick(); release_one_chopstick(); } Can this plan lead to a deadlock? Explain your answer.
questions.answer: No. Deadlock cannot occur because there are enough chopsticks to guarantee that at least one of the 3 diners will be able to get the 2 chopsticks that he/she needs. Once that diner finishes, he/she will release their chopsticks for someone else. So, everyone will finish.

questions.text: Q17. (Read above problem first) Suppose, now instead of 3 diners, we have 'D' number of diners. Furthermore, each diner may acquire different number of chopsticks. Now, each dinners protocol is displayed below: int s; int num_sticks = my_chopsticks_requirement(); while (! had_enough_to_eat()) { for (s=0; s <num_sticks; s++) { acquire_one_chopstick(); } eat(); for (s=0; s <num_sticks; s++) { release_one_chopstick(); } } what is the smallest number of chopsticks (in terms of C and D), needed to ensure that deadlock cannot occur? Explain your answer.
questions.answer: C-D+1. This guarantees that every dinner can get all but one of the chopsticks it needs (C‑D), with one additional chopstick to guarantee that at least one dinner gets all of the chopsticks it needs. Example, suppose D=2 and diner_1 requires 1 chopstick and diner_2 requires 11 chopsticks. Therefore C = 12. So, C‑D+1 = 12‑2+1 = 11. So maximum chopstick requirement is satisfied.

questions.text: what are the different states of process and explain the transitions between them (when does a process moves from one state to other)?
questions.answer: different states of process: 1. Running: The process is being executed. 2. Ready: The process is waiting to be assigned to a processor(waiting to be scheduled). 3. Blocked: suspended, not ready to run Apart from the above states there are two other states also: a. New: The process is being created. b. Terminate: The process has finished execution. Transitions from one state to other: 1. Ready to Running: When it is time to select a process to run, the operating system move the processes from the ready state to the running state. 2. Running to Ready: When the time slot for the process expires or if an interrupt signal occurs, then the operating system shifts the running process to the ready state. 3. Running to Blocked: A process is put into the waiting state if the process needs an event to occur, or an I/O device is to read. 4. Blocked to Ready: A process in the blocked state is moved to the ready state when the event for which it has been waiting has completed.

questions.text: What is difference between process and thread?
questions.answer: Processes:- • When any program is in execution ,it is called process. • Process takes more time for create, terminate and to context switch. • The execution of other processes will not be impacted if one process is blocked. • Child processes are unaffected by changes to the parent process. • Processes do not share data with each other. Threads:- • A segment of process is called thread. •  Thread takes less time for create, terminate and to context switch. • All other user-level threads are also blocked if one of those threads is blocked. • Any changes to the main thread may have an impact on the behaviour of the other threads of the process because all threads of the same process share address space and other resources. • Data is shared between threads.

questions.text: Q16. explain the difference between Preemptive Scheduling and Non-Preemptive Scheduling. Give examples of scheduling policies for each of them.
questions.answer: Ans-> In Preemptive Scheduling, the resources are allocated to the process for a limited amount of time and then taken away, and the process is again placed back in the ready queue if that process still has CPU burst time remaining. That process stays in the ready queue till it gets its next chance to executed. Algorithms based on preemptive scheduling are: Round Robin (RR), Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF), Priority (preemptive version), etc. Non-Preemptive Scheduling: In this scheduling, once the resources (CPU cycles) are allocated to a process, the process holds the CPU till it gets terminated or reaches a waiting state. Algorithms based on non-preemptive scheduling are: Shortest Job First (SJF basically non preemptive) and Priority (non-preemptive version), etc.

questions.text: Q40. A processor uses 36 bit physical addresses and 32 bit virtual addresses, with a page frame size of 4 Kbytes. Each page table entry is of size 4 bytes. A three level page table is used for virtual to physical address translation, where the virtual address is used as follows • Bits 30-31 are used to index into the first level page table • Bits 21-29 are used to index into the second level page table • Bits 12-20 are used to index into the third level page table, and • Bits 0-11 are used as offset within the page The number of bits required for addressing the next level page table (or page frame) in the page table entry of the first, second and third level page tables are respectively (A) 20, 20 and 20 (B) 24, 24 and 24 (C) 24, 24 and 20 (D) 25, 25 and 24
questions.answer:
Virtual address size = 32 bits
Physical address size = 36 bits
Physical memory size = 2^36 bytes
Page frame size = 4K bytes = 2^12 bytes
No. of bits required to access physical memory frame = 36 – 12 = 24
So in third level of page table, 24 bits are required to access an entry.
9 bits of virtual address are used to access second level page table entry and size of pages in second level is 4 bytes. So size of second level page table is (2^9)*4 = 2^11 bytes. It means there are (2^36)/(2^11) possible locations to store this page table. Therefore the second page table requires 25 bits to address it. Similarly, the third page table needs 25 bits to address it.

Q43. Explain demand paging?
questions.answer:
Demand paging is a method that loads pages into memory on demand. This method is mostly used in virtual memory. In this, a page is only brought into memory when a location on that particular page is referenced during execution.

The following steps are generally followed:

1. Attempt to access the page.
2. If the page is valid (in memory) then continue processing instructions as normal. If a page is invalid then a page-fault trap occurs.
3. Check if the memory reference is a valid reference to a location on secondary memory. If not, the process is terminated (illegal memory access). Otherwise, we have to page in the required page.
4. Schedule disk operation to read the desired page into main memory.
5. Restart the instruction that was interrupted by the operating system trap

questions.text: Q44. List the steps needed to handle page fault.
questions.answer:
1. The memory address requested is first checked, to make sure it was a valid memory request.
2. If the reference was invalid, the process is terminated. Otherwise, the page must be paged in.
3. A free frame is located, possibly from a free-frame list.
4. A disk operation is scheduled to bring in the necessary page from disk. (This will usually block the process on an I/O wait, allowing some other process to use the CPU in the meantime.)
5. When the I/O operation is complete, the process’s page table is updated with the new frame number, and the invalid bit is changed to indicate that this is now a valid page reference.
6. The instruction that caused the page fault must now be restarted from the beginning, (as soon as this process gets another turn on the CPU.)

questions.text: Q23. What conditions must be met in order to solve the critical-section problem?
questions.answer:
The requirements are: 1. Mutual exclusion. If process Pi is executing in its critical 
section, then no other processes can be executing in their critical section. 2. Progress. If no 
process is executing in its critical section and some processes wish to enter their critical section, 
then only those processes that are not executing in their remainder sections can participate in the 
decision on which will enter its CS next, and this selection cannot be postponed indefinitely. (No 
process should have to wait forever to enter its critical section. 3. Bounded waiting. There exists 
a bound, or limit, on the number of times that other processes are allowed to enter their critical 
sections after a process has made a request to enter its critical section and before that request is 
granted.

questions.text: Q30. Disabling interrupts was one of the earlier methods proposed for the implementation of locks. Discuss the flaws in this approach.
questions.answer: This approach allows any calling thread to perform a preview of a pre-village operation (turning interrupts on and off), which is quite a risky thing. A greedy program could call lock() at the beginning of its execution and thus monopolize the processor or a malicious program could call lock() and go into an endless loop, and OS will never regain its control of the system. This method will not work in multiprocessor scenarios. If multiple threads are running on different CPUs and each tries to enter the same critical section, even if the interrupts are disabled, the threads will be able to run on other processors and can enter the critical section. This approach can be inefficient. Compared to normal instruction execution, code that masks or unmasks interrupts tends to be executed slowly by modern CPUs.

First, is, when a single thread is running and grabs and releases the lock, what is the overhead of doing so? Another is the case where multiple threads are contending for the lock on a single CPU. questions.text: Q32. Why can the producer-consumer problem be solved by mutex
questions.answer: Mutex is used to solve the producer-consumer problem as mutex helps in mutual exclusion. It stops multiple processes from accessing the critical section. Mutexes only have binary values, 0 and 1, therefore, whenever a process tries to enter the critical section code, it first uses the wait operation to check the mutex value. Wait(mutex): Wait(mutex) reduces mutex's value by 1. Consequently, let's say that a process P1 tries to enter the critical region when the mutex value is 1. P1 performs wait(mutex), which lowers the value of mutex. When P1 enters the code's crucial region, the mutex's value now changes to 0. Now, if Process P2 tries to enter the critical area, it will attempt to lower the mutex value once more. The mutex value, however, is already 0. As a result, wait(mutex) won't run, and P2 will continue to wait for P1 to exit the critical section. Now, imagine that P2 executes signal to exit the critical section (mutex). Signal(mutex): signal(mutex) raises mutex's value by 1. Mutex value once more rises to 1. Now, by executing wait, the process P2 that was in a busy-waiting state will be able to enter the critical section (mutex). Therefore, mutex aids in the processes' mutual exclusion.

questions.text: How would you improve performance when using semaphores?
questions.answer:
Ans:
There are a few ways that you could improve performance when using semaphores:
1. Use a lock-free algorithm – this will allow your program to avoid the overhead of acquiring and 
releasing locks
2. Use a priority queue – this will ensure that the threads with the highest priority are able to acquire the 
semaphore first
3. Use a fair semaphore – this will ensure that all threads have a fair chance of acquiring the semaphore, 
instead of one thread hogging the semaphore and preventing other threads from making progress

questions.answer: Deadlock is a situation when two or more processes wait for each other to finish and none of them ever finish. Consider an example when two trains are coming toward each other on same track and there is only one track, none of the trains can move once they are in front of each other. Similar situation occurs in operating systems when there are two or more processes hold some resources and wait for resources held by other(s).

questions.text: Q10. A system is having 3 user processes P1, P2 and P3 where P1 requires 21 units of resource R, P2 requires 31 units of resource R, P3 requires 41 units of resource R. The minimum number of units of R that ensures no deadlock is ?
questions.answer: In worst case, the number of units that each process holds = One less than its maximum demand. So, Process P1 holds 20 units of resource R; Process P2 holds 30 units of resource R; Process P3 holds 40 units of resource R. Thus, Maximum number of units of resource R that ensures deadlock = 20 + 30 + 40 = 90. Minimum number of units of resource R that ensures no deadlock = 90 + 1 = 91.

questions.text: Q11. How to prevent deadlock?
questions.answer:
1. Mutual Exclusion: When you have sharable resources, there will be no fight for resources, which will prevent deadlock conditions.
2. Hold and Wait: In this condition, a process holding resources is waiting for other resources. But there are ways to eliminate this condition:
   a) When the process beforehand specifies the resources it requires. In this way, the process doesn’t have to wait for allocation.
   b) By releasing all the resources the process is currently holding and then making a new request.
3. No pre-emption: Preemption means temporary interruption of program execution. Normally processes can’t be preempted. Suppose some process P1 wants a resource R1 held by process P2. This situation will lead to a deadlock state. But to avoid deadlock, the process P2 is preempted, and resource R1 could be released and given to process P1. Then we can prevent deadlock.
4. Circular Wait: We can eliminate this circular wait condition by giving priority to each resource. A process accesses the resources in increasing order of priority. If a request is made for a low-priority resource (being held by some other resource), the request will be considered invalid.

Problem on bankers algo  A single processor system has three resource types X, Y and Z, which are shared by three processes. There are 5 units of each resource type. Consider the following scenario, where the column alloc denotes the number of units of each resource type allocated to each process, and the column request denotes the number of units of each resource type requested by a process in order to complete execution. Which of these processes will finish LAST? 1. P0 2. P1 3. P2 4. None of the above since the system is in a deadlock
questions.answer: Solution- According to question- Total = [ X Y Z ] = [ 5 5 5 ] Total_Alloc = [ X Y Z ] = [5 4 3] Available = Total – Total_Alloc = [ 5 5 5 ] – [5 4 3] = [ 0 1 2 ] Step-01: With the instances available currently, only the requirement of the process P1 can be satisfied. So, process P1 is allocated the requested resources. It completes its execution and then free up the instances of resources held by it. Then, Available = [ 0 1 2 ] + [ 2 0 1] = [ 2 1 3 ] Step-02: With the instances available currently, only the requirement of the process P0 can be satisfied. So, process P0 is allocated the requested resources. It completes its execution and then free up the instances of resources held by it. Then- Available = [ 2 1 3 ] + [ 1 2 1 ] = [ 3 3 4 ] Step-03: With the instances available currently, the requirement of the process P2 can be satisfied. So, process P2 is allocated the requested resources. It completes its execution and then free up the instances of resources held by it. Then- Available = [ 3 3 4 ] + [ 2 2 1 ] = [ 5 5 5 ] Thus, There exists a safe sequence P1, P0, P2 in which all the processes can be executed. So, the system is in a safe state. Process P2 will be executed at last. Thus, Option (C) is correct.

questions.text: Q10. what are the different states of process and explain the transitions between them (when does a process moves from one state to other)?
questions.answer: different states of process: 1. Running: The process is being executed. 2. Ready: The process is waiting to be assigned to a processor(waiting to be scheduled). 3. Blocked: suspended, not ready to run Apart from the above states there are two other states also: a. New: The process is being created. b. Terminate: The process has finished execution. Transitions from one state to other: 1. Ready to Running: When it is time to select a process to run, the operating system move the processes from the ready state to the running state. 2. Running to Ready: When the time slot for the process expires or if an interrupt signal occurs, then the operating system shifts the running process to the ready state. 3. Running to Blocked: A process is put into the waiting state if the process needs an event to occur, or an I/O device is to read. 4. Blocked to Ready: A process in the blocked state is moved to the ready state when the event for which it has been waiting has completed.

questions.text: Q12. What is difference between process and thread?
questions.answer: Processes:- When any program is in execution ,it is called process. Process takes more time for create, terminate and to context switch. Threads:- A segment of process is called thread. Thread takes less time for create, terminate and to context switch. All other user-level threads are also blocked if one of those threads is blocked. Any changes to the main thread may have an impact on the behaviour of the other threads of the process because all threads of the same process share address space and other resources. questions.text: explain the difference between Preemptive Scheduling and Non-Preemptive Scheduling. Give examples of scheduling policies for each of them.
questions.answer: In Preemptive Scheduling, the resources are allocated to the process for a limited amount of time and then taken away, and the process is again placed back in the ready queue if that process still has CPU burst time remaining. That process stays in the ready queue till it gets its next chance to executed. Algorithms based on preemptive scheduling are: Round Robin (RR), Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF), Priority (preemptive version), etc. Non-Preemptive Scheduling: In this scheduling, once the resources (CPU cycles) are allocated to a process, the process holds the CPU till it gets terminated or reaches a waiting state. Algorithms based on non-preemptive scheduling are: Shortest Job First (SJF basically non preemptive) and Priority (non-preemptive version), etc.

Q47) Consider a two level paging scheme. The page size is 4 KB and page table entry size is 4 bytes. The size of outer page table is 4 KB. Give the division of virtual address space.
questions.answer:
Given-
• Page size = 4 KB 
• Page table entry size = 4 bytes 
• Page table size = 4 KB 

Let the number of bits in virtual address = n bits


 Number of Bits in Page Offset- 
We have, 
Page size 
= 4 KB 
= 212 B 
Thus, Number of bits in page offset = 12 bits

Process Size- 
Number of bits in virtual address = n bits 
Thus, 
Process size = 2n bytes 

Number of Pages of Process- 
Number of pages the process is divided 
= Process size / Page size 
= 2n B / 4 KB 
= 2n B / 212 B 
= 2n-12 pages

Inner Page Table Size- 
Inner page table keeps track of the frames storing the pages of process. 
Inner page table size 
= Number of entries in inner page table x Page table entry size 
= Number of pages the process is divided x Page table entry size 
= 2n-12 x 4 bytes 
= 2n-12+2 bytes 
= 2n-10 bytes 

Number of Pages of Inner Page Table- 
Number of pages the inner page table is divided 
= Inner page table size / Page size 
= 2n-10 B / 4 KB 
= 2n-10 B / 212 B 
= 2n-22 pages  
= 2n-10-12 

Now, these 2n-22 pages of inner page table are stored in different frames of the main memory. 

Number of Page Table Entries in One Page of Inner Page Table- 
Number of page table entries in one page of inner page table 
= Page size / Page table entry size 
= 4 KB / 4 bytes 
= 1 K 
= 210 entries 

Number of Bits Required to Search an Entry in One Page of Inner Page Table- 
One page of inner page table contains 210 entries. 
Thus, 
Number of bits required to search a particular entry in one page of inner page table = 10 bits 


Outer Page Table Size- 
Outer page table is required to keep track of the frames storing the pages of inner page table. 
Outer page table size 
= Number of entries in outer page table x Page table entry size 
= Number of pages the inner page table is divided x Page table entry size 
= 2n-22 x 4 bytes 
= 2n-22+2 bytes 
= 2n-20 bytes 
But we are given outer page table size = 4 KB 
Thus, 
2n-20 bytes = 4 KB 
2n-20 = 212 
n – 20 = 12 
∴ n = 32 
Thus, number of bits in virtual address = 32 bits 



Number of Bits Required to Search an Entry in Outer Page Table- 
Method-01: 
Number of bits required to search a particular entry in outer page table 
= Number of bits in virtual address – (Number of bits required to search an entry in inner page table + Number of bits in page offset) 
= 32 bits – (10 bits + 12 bits) 
= 32 bits – 22 bitS
= 10 bits 

Method-02: 
Number of entries in outer page table 
= Number of pages the inner page table is divided 
= 2n-22 
= 232-22 
= 210 
Thus, Number of bits required to search a particular entry in outer page table = 10 bits

questions.text: Q30. Disabling interrupts was one of the earlier methods proposed for the implementation of locks. Discuss the flaws in this approach.
questions.answer:
This approach allows any calling thread to perform a preview of a pre-village operation (turning interrupts on and off), which is quite a risky thing. A greedy program could call lock() at the beginning of its execution and thus monopolize the processor or a malicious program could call lock() and go into an endless loop, and OS will never regain its control of the system.

This method will not work in multiprocessor scenarios. If multiple threads are running on different CPUs and each tries to enter the same critical section, even if the interrupts are disabled, the threads will be able to run on other processors and can enter the critical section.

This approach can be inefficient. Compared to normal instruction execution, code that masks or unmasks interrupts tends to be executed slowly by modern CPUs.

For these reasons, turning off interrupts is only used in limited contexts as a solution for mutual exclusion.

questions.text: Q32. Why can the producer-consumer problem be solved by mutex
questions.answer:
Mutex is used to solve the producer-consumer problem as mutex helps in mutual exclusion. It stops multiple processes from accessing the critical section. Mutexes only have binary values, 0 and 1, therefore, whenever a process tries to enter the critical section code, it first uses the wait operation to check the mutex value.
Wait(mutex):
Wait(mutex) reduces mutex's value by 1. Consequently, let's say that a process P1 tries to enter the critical region when the mutex value is 1. P1 performs wait(mutex), which lowers the value of mutex. When P1 enters the code's crucial region, the mutex's value now changes to 0.

Now, if Process P2 tries to enter the critical area, it will attempt to lower the mutex value once more. The mutex value, however, is already 0. As a result, wait(mutex) won't run, and P2 will continue to wait for P1 to exit the critical section.

Now, imagine that P2 executes signal to exit the critical section (mutex).

Signal(mutex):
signal(mutex) raises mutex's value by 1. Mutex value once more rises to 1. Now, by executing wait, the process P2 that was in a busy-waiting state will be able to enter the critical section (mutex). Therefore, mutex aids in the processes' mutual exclusion.

Wait and signal operations on mutex are present in the aforementioned section in both the Producer process code and the Consumer process code, which aids in mutual exclusion and fixes the Producer Consumer problem.

section can enter its critical section next.

allowed to enter their critical sections after a process has made a request.

questions.text: Q10. what are the different states of process and explain the transitions between them (when does a process moves from one state to other)?
questions.answer:
different states of process:
Running: The process is being executed.
Ready: The process is waiting to be assigned to a processor(waiting to be scheduled).
Blocked: suspended, not ready to run
Apart from the above states there are two other states also:
New: The process is being created.
Terminate: The process has finished execution.
Transitions from one state to other:
Ready to Running: When it is time to select a process to run, the operating system move the processes from the ready state to the running state.
Running to Ready: When the time slot for the process expires or if an interrupt signal occurs, then the operating system shifts the running process to the ready state.
Running to Blocked: A process is put into the waiting state if the process needs an event to occur, or an I/O device is to read.
Blocked to Ready: A process in the blocked state is moved to the ready state when the event for which it has been waiting has completed.

questions.text: Q16.  explain the difference between Preemptive Scheduling and Non-Preemptive Scheduling. Give examples of scheduling policies for each of them.
questions.answer:
In Preemptive Scheduling, the resources are allocated to the process for a limited amount of time and then taken away, and the process is again placed back in the ready queue if that process still has CPU burst time remaining. That process stays in the ready queue till it gets its next chance to executed.

Algorithms based on preemptive scheduling are: Round Robin (RR), Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF), Priority (preemptive version), etc.
Non-Preemptive Scheduling: In this scheduling, once the resources (CPU cycles) are allocated to a process, the process holds the CPU till it gets terminated or reaches a waiting state.
Algorithms based on non-preemptive scheduling are: Shortest Job First (SJF basically non preemptive) and Priority (non-preemptive version), etc.

What are the different types of Kernel?
questions.answer:
Monolithic Kernels –In this architecture of kernel, all the system services were packaged into a single system module which lead to poor maintainability and huge size of kernel.
Microkernels – They follow the modular approach of architecture. Maintainability became easier with this model as only the concerned module is to be altered and loaded for every function. This model also keeps a tab on the ever growing code size of the kernel.

questions.text: What is the difference between Kernel and OS?
questions.answer:
Kernel is a system program that controls all programs running on the computer. The kernel is basically a bridge between the software and hardware of the system.

Operating System: Operating system is a system program that runs on the computer to provide an interface to the computer user so that they can easily operate on the computer.

questions.text: Consider a primitive disk that has 50 tracks. A seek takes 5 ms (on average) to move the arm head per track. On an average, without optimization (to try to put sequential file data in blocks with close proximity) two logically consecutive blocks in a file will be about 10 tracks apart. however, with an optimization attempt to cluster related blocks, the mean inter-block distance can be reduced to 2 tracks. If the rotational latency is 50 ms and the transfer time is 15 ms per block, how long does it take to read a 50-block file in both cases.
questions.answer: It takes 15 msec to transfer one block, thus transferring 50 blocks takes 750 msec. If the average number of tracks to move is 10, then at 5 msec per track this will take 2500 (5x10x50) msec for a 50 block file. Lastly, the rotational latency is 50 msec and is added for every block, thus total is 2500 msec rotational delay. Thus the non-optimized solution for this problem is 750 + 2,500 +  2500 = 5750 msec to transfer a 50 block file. Optimization only alters the mean interblock distance to 2 tracks and thus reduces seek time from 2500 to 500 (5x2x50) msec. Thus the total time for an optimized disk is (750 + 500 +2,500  =) 3750 msec.

questions.text: Base register of segment 0
questions.answer:
To calculate this, find a valid reference to segment 0. For example:
VA 0x00000005 (decimal: 5) --> VALID in SEG0: 0x00000205 (decimal: 517)
Here you can see that virtual address 5 translates to physical address 517. Subtracting the offset into segment 0 (5) from 517 gets us 512, which must be the base address (0x400 in hex).

questions.text: Bounds register of segment 0
questions.answer:
For this, you need to find (in the best case) two references, one that is at virtual address N and is valid, and one that is at address N+1 but is not valid; that will tell us the bound precisely. And hence:
VA 0x0000001d (decimal: 29) --> VALID in SEG0: 0x0000021d (decimal: 541)
VA 0x0000001e (decimal: 30) --> SEGMENTATION VIOLATION (SEG0)
This tells us that any virtual address from 0 through 29 is valid, whereas 30 is not. Hence, the size of segment zero is 30, which we thus conclude is the bound. If you want the physical address instead, it is base plus size, or 542.

questions.text: Base register of segment 1
questions.answer:
Similar to the question above, but remember that segment 1 goes backwards:
VA 0x0000006c (decimal: 108) --> VALID in SEG1: 0x000003ec (decimal: 1004)
Thus, if 108 maps to 1004, we know that 127 (the last valid byte of the virtual address space) would map to 1023 (add 19 to 108 gets us 127; thus add 19 to 1004 to get 1023). Hence, the base (as described in the notes) would be 1024, just beyond the end of where the backward-growing segment lies.

questions.text: Bounds register of segment 1
questions.answer:
The bound here is harder, because it is imprecise.
VA 0x00000050 (decimal: 80) --> SEGMENTATION VIOLATION (SEG1)
VA 0x00000058 (decimal: 88) --> VALID in SEG1: 0x000003d8 (decimal: 984)
As you can see, 80 goes too far backwards, but 88 is fine. With 88, the size must at least allow 88 through 127 to be valid; thus 40 bytes is the minimum segment size. It clearly could also be that 81 is valid, which adds 7 more bytes into the segment size, or 47. Thus, the size of this segment is between 40 and 47, inclusive

questions.answer: A TLB valid bit refers to whether a TLB entry has a valid translation within it. When a system boots, for example, a common initial state for each TLB entry is to be set to invalid, because no address translations are yet cached there. Once virtual memory is enabled, and once programs start running and accessing their virtual address spaces, the TLB is slowly populated, and thus valid entries soon fill the TLB. In a page table, when a page-table entry (PTE) is marked invalid, it means that the page has not been allocated by the process, and should not be accessed by a correctly-working program. The usual response when an invalid page is accessed is to trap the OS, which will respond by killing the process.

With respect to use of Condition Variable (CV), note that in addition to the CV, the wait() call takes a mutex lock as its second argument. State the dynamics of wait( ) call and explain the reason behind involving mutex lock in this design. Also briefly state the need for using a while() loop for the predicate check in the calling of the wait() operation.
questions.answer:
The wait() on CV, puts the caller to sleep + releases the lock (atomically), otherwise how could another thread acquire the lock and change the state and/or signal it to wake up? Also if putting to sleep + releases the lock both is not done atomically then also there is a race condition so that is also taken care by this call. Before returning after being woken up, wait() re-acquires the lock, thus ensuring that anytime the waiting thread is running between the lock acquired at the beginning of the wait sequence and the lock release at the end, it holds the lock. This design of wait() call thus is very convenient for application use so that programmer need not worry about concurrency issues coming up.
When a condition variable is signaled to wake up a thread, it is removed from the wait queue but before that thread reacquires the mutex, another thread may be given CPU time (and potentially the mutex). As a result, the shared state may be updated before the waking up thread reacquires the mutex. Therefore, the thread must do another check when it actually acquires the mutex to ensure the condition it needs to proceed is still true.

questions.text: State 2 main benefits of multithreading? What are the possible sources of overhead associated with multithreading?
questions.answer:
There are two main benefits of multithreading, namely parallelization and concurrency (on single CPU) i.e is the hiding of I/O latency.
Adding threads make sense if you have fewer threads than you have cores or if you are performing many I/O requests. Adding threads can lead to pure overhead otherwise.
While new threads require less memory than new processes, they still do require memory. This means that threads cannot be made for free, and in fact thread creation is often quite expensive. In addition, thread synchronization can add more overhead to the system, in terms of the CPU cycles and memory that must be consumed to represent and operate synchronously.

questions.text: Briefly state why and how the OS uses a timer interrupt
questions.answer: Timer interrupt is mainly used to help OS regain the CPU after specified period. Its value is set by kernel via privileged instruction and a timer interrupt happens when the timer counts down to 0.  The timer interrupt handler in kernel invokes the process scheduler to decide which process is executed next. It is also helpful in implementation of certain scheduling strategies like round robin.

questions.text: Imagine a new hardware mechanism that counts the total number of instructions that have been executed and then raises an interrupt after some fixed number of instructions have passed. Is the ICIR a good alternative (to timer interrupt) mechanism for the OS? Why or why not?
questions.answer: It does provide basic mechanism as instead of setting the timer interrupt to go off say every 10 ms, with the ICIR, we set an interrupt to go off every so many instructions. However, since instruction times may vary, ICIR may go off at irregular intervals making it a little harder for the scheduling policy to keep track of how long each process had run.

questions.text: What is shortest-time-to-completion first, or STCF scheduling policy and for which metric it is optimal. Why do we rarely see it implemented?
questions.answer: STCF picks the job with the least time left to run for scheduling on CPU. It is the preemptive generalization of SJF. It provides optimal turnaround time. It is rarely used because in general (most cases) it is not possible to know the job run time in advance.

questions.text: Sometimes a TLB will contain two entries that have the same physical page number– when?
questions.answer: any time two separate processes are sharing a page of memory, the TLB will have two entries that refer to the same physical page

questions.text: Sometimes a TLB may contain two entries that have the same virtual page number – when?
questions.answer: TLB will hold entries with the same virtual page number when two different processes have entries in the TLB at the same time.

questions.text: Do either or both of these cases above (a & b) require extra hardware support from the system to work properly?
questions.answer: yes, both do. In the first case, we have sharing, and hence undoubtedly need protection bits. In the second, we need to distinguish entries with the same VPN, and hence need an address-space identifier of some kind.

questions.text: Why is LRU considered a good page replacement policy? Describe a case where it performs badly.
questions.answer: because of the principle of locality of reference, LRU is better at keeping those pages which are recently (and so probably frequently) used. So in general it can minimize page faults however, cases like “looping sequential” workload where we refer to a sequence of pages in repetition (with no. of page frames lesser than the total pages in sequence), it results in page fault in every access.

questions.text: How are reference bits used to implement an approximate LRU?
questions.answer: Upon a memory reference to a page, algorithm assumes that the hardware will set a bit saying that the given page has been accessed. The OS, when it needs a page, will then sweep through the pages of memory in a circular (or clock-like) fashion, looking for a page that has not been accessed recently (i.e., its reference bit has not been set). In doing the sweep, the OS also clears the bits as it examines them, and hence in the worst case will sweep all the way around before replacing a page (in the case that all pages had been accessed).

questions.text: Using first fit allocation, explain whether all requests succeed?
questions.answer: First fit fails upon the fourth request, for 35 bytes. Why? Because the 10 byte chunk is used by request 1, the 20 byte chunk used by the 15-byte request 2 (leaving a 5-byte chunk), and then the 40-byte chunk gets used by request 3 (leaving a 30-byte chunk). Hence, when the 35-byte request rolls around, there is a 5-byte, 30-byte, and 10-byte chunk, leading to failure.

questions.text: Using best fit allocation, explain whether all requests succeed?
questions.answer: Yes. Request 1 is served by the 10-byte chunk, request 2 by the 20-byte chunk (leaving 5), request 3 by the last 10-byte chunk, and request 4 by the 40-byte chunk (leaving 5).

questions.text: Assume we divide the heap into fixed-sized units of size S. Also assume that we never get a request for a unit larger than S. Thus, for any request you receive, you will return a single block of size S, if you have any free blocks. What kind of fragmentation can occur in this situation, and why is this bad?
questions.answer: Internal fragmentation may occur. This is bad simply because it potentially wastes space, e.g., if all requests are for 1 byte, S-1 bytes will be wasted per request. It is called internal fragmentation because the waste is “internal” in the block that has been allocated.

questions.text: Now consider a non-standard Unix file system, which instead of using inodes, instead stores most information about a file in the directory entry for that file. We call our new system the Inode-Free File System, or IFFS. Now compare the number of reads it would take to read a single block from the same file /this/path/is/toolong in IFFS.
questions.answer: 5 disk reads as there is no inode now only data block.

questions.text: IFFS doesn’t support hard links. Why do you think so (explain)?
questions.answer: In the standard file system, a hard link is represented by having different directory entries (i.e., different path names) point to the same inode; in this way, a user can refer to any of those path name to access the same inode and thus the same data. Thus, inodes serve as a useful single point of indirection mapping file names to data. In IFFS, there is no way for different pathnames to point to the same exact file. Although different directory entries could contain the same pointers to the same data blocks, there is no mechanism to keep the directory entries consistent with each other; if the user appends, truncates, or deletes the file through one name, the other versions will not be updated. Thus, hard links cannot be supported.

questions.text: Explain the “shortest seek time first” (SSTF) disk scheduling algorithm and its primary problem.
questions.answer: Shortest seek time first (SSTF) algorithm selects the disk I/O request which requires the least disk seek movement (track change) from its current position thus reducing the total seek time. But it does not take into account rotation time. Its primary problem is that it can cause starvation - If there a steady stream of requests to the tracks near to the current head position then requests to any other tracks will starve.

questions.text: You develop a new algorithm, called two-queue SSTF. The idea is simple: you put the first N requests into the first of two disk scheduling queues, and start by servicing those requests in SSTF-based order. However, as the next so many requests arrive into the system, they are put into a different “second” queue. No request in this other queue is serviced until all of the requests in the first queue have been. At this point, the second queue starts getting serviced (again in SSTF order), and requests that arrive during this phase are put into the first queue (and not serviced until all requests in the second queue have been). And so forth. How does this two-queue policy compare to SSTF
questions.answer: The primary difference is that this algorithm prevents starvation; all requests in one queue (of which there are a finite number) are guaranteed to be serviced before any requests in the second queue. A secondary difference is that it may have worse performance because it could incur more seeks.

questions.text: with respect to concurrency bugs, what is the primary difference in the causes of non-deadlock bugs vs. deadlock bugs?
questions.answer: non-deadlock bugs are caused because of not using sufficient synchronization primitives (like locks, CVs) leading to atomicity or ordering violation. Deadlock bugs are caused because of improperly using those primitives especially locks leading to circular wait or hold and wait situation.

questions.text: For deadlock to occur, four conditions must hold: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait. If any one condition does not hold, no deadlock can occur. Assume we want to allow “preemption”, and thus get out of deadlocks; in other words, if a deadlock is detected, we will forcibly take a lock away from a thread; by repeatedly doing this, we will eventually undo the deadlock. State any two distinct problems that can get introduced by this preemptive approach?
questions.answer:
Various problems may be introduced:
1) livelock situation where there is repeated taking away and re-allocation of resources but no actual progress
2) can cause atomicity violation if the resources preempted are locks for imposing mutual exclusion; incorrect execution, if the resources taken away are used for ordering tasks; incorrect execution if the resource cannot be preempted in between (e.g., a printer)

questions.text: A system is having 3 user processes P1, P2 and P3 where P1 requires 21 units of resource R, P2 requires 31 units of resource R, P3 requires 41 units of resource R. Calculate the minimum number of units of R that ensures no deadlock?

In worst case, the number of units that each process holds = One less than its maximum  demand
So,
Process P1 holds 20 units of resource R
Process P2 holds 30 units of resource R
Process P3 holds 40 units of resource R 
Thus, Minimum number of units of resource R that ensures no deadlock = 20 + 30 + 40 +1 = 91

questions.answer: In the following pseudo code, the level variables take on values up to N − 1, each representing a distinct "waiting room" before the critical section. To acquire a lock, process with pid executes following for ℓ from 0 to N − 1 exclusive level[pid] ← ℓ last_to_enter[ℓ] ← pid while(last_to_enter[ℓ] = pid and there exists k ≠ pid,such that level[k] ≥ ℓ) //wait To release the lock upon exiting the critical section, process pid sets level[pid] to −1.

questions.answer: Strengths – simple, fast, provides protection, little space overhead Weaknesses – not flexible, doesn’t support sparse address space, can have either internal or external fragmentation
